title: Drew Jackson & Chris McGrath — Beagle+ at LSC ITC 2025: a public-legal-education nonprofit's RAG chatbot, with accuracy and cost figures
pub: LSC Innovations in Technology Conference 2025 (Phoenix), streamed session, LSC YouTube channel
author: Drew Jackson · Chris McGrath

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, bounded deployment and materially extends the cluster with an operating example: a RAG chatbot limited to legal information, subject to comprehensive human review, privacy and usage controls, jurisdiction-specific content, and escalation to human help. Its reported reach supports scalable task-level access gains, while its advice boundary and referral model reinforce that such gains do not amount to general legal competence or complete access to a remedy.

kp.k: Justice-gap evidence motivates scalable public legal guidance
kp.d: Jackson frames Beagle Plus as a response to unmet legal need across income levels, citing a 2021 Statistics Canada survey: 33% contacted a legal professional, 51% went online, 70% found internet searching helpful, and 63% found contacting a community organization helpful. People's Law School, a nine-person nonprofit serving British Columbia, sees the chatbot as a way to deliver trusted, plain-language guidance at volumes its staff could not otherwise support.

kp.k: Deployment extends an earlier decision-tree chatbot
kp.d: The speakers describe replacing the earlier Beagle, launched in March 2020, with a generative-AI chatbot available through two websites and Facebook. They report about 6,000 conversations over 11 months, approximately 600 monthly. The transcript gives inconsistent launch timing: one statement says February 2023, while another says February 15 of the previous year in this 2025 session.

kp.k: RAG grounds answers in jurisdiction-specific nonprofit content
kp.d: The system uses GPT-4o, system instructions and retrieved website material to generate British Columbia-focused responses. It first simplifies the user query using conversation history, retrieves five to 10 snippets of up to 400 words, and uses different prompts depending on whether relevant content exists. Website content is refreshed nightly. McGrath's suggestion that whole-site input might replace this architecture within a few years is a prediction, not a demonstrated capability.

kp.k: Chatbot translates legal information into actionable public guidance
kp.d: Selected real-conversation examples illustrate jurisdictional clarification, empathetic responses, plain-language explanations, contextual discussion of rights, and links to forms, legal help and complaint-letter tools. Jackson argues that the system can acknowledge steps already attempted and explain why consulting a lawyer may add value. These examples demonstrate the speakers' account of capabilities, rather than measured legal outcomes.

kp.k: User feedback indicates helpfulness, not comparative professional effectiveness
kp.d: The speakers report 79% helpfulness among respondents over 11 months, with 1,691 responses from approximately 6,000 conversations, described as a 30% response rate. Website feedback attracts under 1%. Jackson explicitly cautions against treating this self-selected feedback as equivalent to the more sophisticated Statistics Canada study reporting 77% helpfulness for legal professionals.

kp.k: Internal testing reports substantial legal-accuracy improvements
kp.d: The speakers report approximately 70% legal accuracy for an April 2023 GPT-3.5 prototype without RAG, 80% by October with RAG, 90% by December using GPT-4 and further changes, and eventually 99% after prompt refinement on approximately 50 difficult questions. Lawyers repeatedly evaluated this test set, drawn from actual earlier inquiries. Accuracy meant substantive correctness about legal rights and options, allowing inconsequential mistakes; these are internal development results, not an independent benchmark.

kp.k: Lawyer review drives continuing correction of production errors
kp.d: As of December 2024, the speakers report approximately 5,300 accurate conversations and 54 inaccurate ones, with every conversation reviewed by a lawyer. They attribute resolution of 22 errors to website changes, four to system-prompt changes, and 28 to a relevance-scoring addition. They explicitly do not claim these corrections establish future 100% accuracy. The feedback loop also improves public website content, illustrated by clarifying whether an eligibility period meant consecutive days.

kp.k: Relevance scoring reduces unsupported answers and scope overreach
kp.d: The system asks the model to score whether retrieved material actually answers the query. Scores zero to six trigger redirection through a question; seven to 10 permit an answer grounded in the material. The speakers credit this change with correcting approximately half of identified inaccurate responses and reducing answers that went beyond scope despite superficially related retrieval results. This is model self-assessment within generation, distinct from subsequent lawyer review.
qs: If the relevant score is zero to six, you have no relevant content that can be used to reply to the user's query
If the relevant score is seven to 10, generate an answer based on the content.
This little tweak here was a big win for us and that looked after half of our inaccurate responses

kp.k: Prompt rules operationalize an information-versus-advice boundary
kp.d: People's Law School permits discussion of options but instructs the chatbot not to recommend a particular next step or assure users that information applies to them. Jackson presents this as the organization's understanding of the boundary, not an authoritative legal determination. Refinements addressed recommendations and a request to draft disability-pension appeal submissions, shifting the latter toward refusal plus general guidance.
qs: You can discuss options and possible next steps. You do not provide legal advice. You do not recommend a particular option or next step. You do not assure the user that the information you provide applies to them.
we think that captures for our sense of this distinction, the critical points.

kp.k: Human review is becoming a scaling constraint
kp.d: Although delivery scales cheaply, reviewing every conversation manually is stretching the legal-content team. The speakers describe early experiments with a product called Fuse in the transcript, building reusable test datasets and using an LLM to score legal-advice content. Scores of eight, nine or 10 would flag conversations for human review. Their expectation of 10- or 100-fold review capacity is explicitly prospective, with lawyers retained for critical cases.

kp.k: Labor dominates costs despite inexpensive model usage
kp.d: The speakers report infrastructure costing under a couple hundred dollars monthly and average OpenAI spending of US$0.03 per conversation, correcting an initial Canadian-dollar attribution and describing the equivalent as C$0.05. They estimate 150–600 hours for technical development, roughly the same for legal review and internal management, 50–100 annual maintenance hours to preserve existing functionality, and 100–300 annual legal-review hours. Development requirements and organizational standards can substantially increase costs.

kp.k: Privacy and usage controls accompany public deployment
kp.d: The speakers rely on OpenAI's API terms commitment not to use transmitted data for training, and scrub personally identifiable information before storing conversations for review. Cloudflare Turnstile screens for human users. Conversations are capped at eight turns, primarily for cost control but also to limit abuse. These are reported implementation safeguards, not claims that all privacy or security risks are eliminated.

kp.k: Forms and multilingual assistance remain development priorities
kp.d: The speakers propose supplying form content to support more reliable assistance after observing unsupported answers to questions about particular form paragraphs. Multilingual replies have received encouraging informal checks from speakers of those languages, but systematic testing, including legal accuracy, remains outstanding. These are prospective extensions rather than validated services at the reported accuracy level.

kp.k: Human referrals and user understanding remain important limitations
kp.d: Responding to audience questions, the speakers acknowledge that some users need more support than a chatbot can offer and emphasize referrals to people. Their interpretation that at least half of negative feedback reflects disagreement with the information is presented as their reading of conversations, not a formal study. They also acknowledge that some users mistake the bot for a person, despite believing most recognize it as automated.

getting people who need people in front of people remains a priority for us across everything we do.

kp.k: Wider adoption requires sharing expertise and jurisdictional grounding
kp.d: In response to an audience question about extending the model elsewhere and improving mainstream AI tools, Jackson advocates openness about the implementation and collaborative efforts to bring nonprofit and legal-aid information into large platforms. He identifies inadequate jurisdictional specificity in platforms and search engines as an ongoing obstacle. The exchange offers a direction for collaboration, not a concrete replication program.

inserting the great information that nonprofits and legal aid agencies provide in these large platforms.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jackson claims that a jurisdiction-specific generative-AI chatbot can expand a small nonprofit's capacity to provide tailored public legal education and help address unmet legal need.
pts.d: Jackson presents Beagle Plus as a means of delivering plain-language information from a trusted community organization at a scale that People's Law School's nine-person team could not match through individual assistance. The presenters report approximately 6,000 conversations over 11 months, or about 600 per month. Further expansion by tenfold or hundredfold is an opportunity rather than a reported result. This is a claim about public legal education and access to justice, not replacement of legal representation.

pts.k: Jackson claims that Beagle Plus can explain rights in context, communicate empathetically, coach users through options, and connect them to practical action and human assistance.
pts.d: His examples include probate guidance and forms, neighbor-noise options, plain-language explanations of annulment and divorce, severance factors, and links to complaint-letter tools. He attributes these capabilities to observed conversations and demonstrations. He argues that acknowledging steps already attempted can make users feel heard, and that links to forms, document builders and legal-help resources can make action more likely. These are claimed capabilities and effects; the presentation does not report measured rates of completed forms, resolved disputes or improved legal outcomes.

pts.k: Jackson and McGrath claim that curated retrieval, stronger models and iterative prompts substantially improved legal accuracy and constrained unsupported answers.
pts.d: The presenters describe a progression from approximately 70% accuracy using GPT-3.5 without retrieval, to 80% with retrieval, to 90% with GPT-4, and then 99% after further refinements. They distinguish a repeated prelaunch test set from subsequent lawyer review of live conversations. McGrath attributes 28 of 54 identified production problems to issues addressed through a prompt asking the model to assess retrieved-content relevance before answering. Jackson also claims that correcting source material in response to chatbot failures improves the underlying website for other users.

pts.k: McGrath predicts that AI-assisted evaluation could greatly expand review capacity while reserving lawyer attention for flagged conversations.
pts.d: At the time of the session, lawyers manually reviewed conversations after users had received the chatbot's responses. The team was experimenting with an evaluation platform to rerun test questions and score outputs for provision of legal advice. McGrath describes tenfold or hundredfold greater review capacity as an optimistic prospective benefit, not an achieved productivity result. The proposed system is automated evaluation and triage for human review, not evidence that every answer is verified before delivery.

pts.k: The presenters identify future opportunities in form assistance and multilingual support, while McGrath predicts that current retrieval infrastructure may eventually become unnecessary.
pts.d: Jackson envisages supplying actual form content so the chatbot can help users navigate forms rather than guess what particular fields require. He reports promising informal checks of answers in languages other than English, but says systematic legal-accuracy testing remains future work. Separately, McGrath predicts that within a few years models may accept an entire website or reliably restrict answers to a specified site without the team's current retrieval process.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source supports usefulness and access claims with service-use metrics, voluntary feedback, conversation examples and a Canadian legal-needs survey.
pts.d: Jackson reports 79% helpfulness among 1,691 respondents across approximately 6,000 conversations, describing the response rate as 30%. He contrasts this with under 1% feedback response on the websites and interprets the chatbot response rate as an engagement indicator. His contextual evidence is a 2021 Statistics Canada survey: 33% contacted a legal professional, 51% went online, and reported helpfulness was 77% for legal professionals, 70% for internet searching and 63% for community organizations. He expressly declines to treat the chatbot's voluntary feedback as equivalent to that survey. Selected actual conversations and a live demo support the claimed capabilities; no systematic legal-outcome study is reported.

pts.k: The reported accuracy rests on internal lawyer evaluation of a repeatedly used test set and live conversation logs.
pts.d: The approximately 50-question development set contained difficult real questions from the earlier chatbot and the organization's lawyer-staffed Q&A service. Legal content developers repeatedly assessed accuracy and helpfulness. For production through December 2024, the presenters report approximately 5,300 accurate conversations and 54 inaccurate ones, with every conversation reviewed by a lawyer. Accuracy meant substantive correctness about rights and options, allowing inconsequential mistakes. They report addressing 22 errors through website changes, four through other prompt changes and 28 through the relevance-scoring prompt. They explicitly say resolving those identified cases does not establish 100% future accuracy. This is internal service evaluation, not an independent benchmark or a measured hallucination rate.

pts.k: The cost claim distinguishes inexpensive model usage from substantial development, management and legal-review labor.
pts.d: McGrath reports average OpenAI spending of US$0.03 per conversation, calculated by dividing total OpenAI charges by conversation count. The speakers clarify that this is US rather than Canadian currency. Basic infrastructure for their broader activities is reported as under a couple hundred dollars per month. Rough estimates are 150–600 hours of technical development, a similar amount for legal review and internal management, 50–100 maintenance hours annually to preserve existing functionality, and 100–300 annual legal-review hours. These figures do not establish an all-in three-cent service cost.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The operational claims concern roughly 11 months of deployment by the 2025 session, following development in 2023; the transcript contains an inconsistent launch-year statement.
pts.d: The session repeatedly describes 11 months of operation, gives production review figures through December 2024, and later places launch on February 15 of the preceding year, implying February 2024. One earlier statement instead says February 2023. The development sequence describes April 2023 testing without retrieval, October testing with retrieval, and December testing with GPT-4. Future review automation, form support and systematic multilingual testing were not established production results at the session.

pts.k: The claimed service benefits depend on jurisdiction-specific content, ongoing maintenance and a deliberate boundary between information and advice.
pts.d: The deployed system uses GPT-4o, retrieves material from People's Law School websites and refreshes its database nightly. The relevance prompt instructs it to answer from content scored seven to ten and otherwise redirect with a question. The presenters' operational definition permits explaining options but forbids recommending a particular step or assuring users that information applies to them. They also constrained drafting of specific legal submissions. These are their stated service boundaries, not a legal ruling about the information/advice distinction. Manual review was already straining staff capacity, qualifying the scaling claim, and they acknowledge that some users need human support.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are British Columbia residents with everyday legal problems, public-legal-education staff and lawyers, and potentially other jurisdictions' legal-help organizations.
pts.d: Jackson situates the tool within a province of five million people and a nonprofit reaching more than a million residents annually through its broader services. Intended beneficiaries include people unable to afford counsel, low-income users and the 'missing middle,' users seeking practical self-help, and potentially speakers of languages other than English. Staff and legal content developers gain a scalable public-facing channel but take on development, retrospective review and continuous content improvement. Lawyers remain referral destinations for users needing individualized help and reviewers of problematic outputs. Other nonprofits and legal-aid agencies may learn from the project, but the speakers emphasize jurisdiction-specific content and offer no established universal deployment model or prediction of law-firm job displacement.
